tonight.headline: Nothing to do here today, and that is the finding
body: Week 3 has not started. The first kickoff is Atlanta–Green Bay on Thursday at 18:15 Mexico City, and nothing you own plays in it. ESPN projects you 132.9 to 120.0 over Footballers.

Four of your roster slots changed hands six hours ago when waivers processed, and those claims left you at waiver priority 10 of 10. The lineup is already correct. The honest recommendation this morning is to touch nothing and read the Friday practice reports.

case.label: What the waiver run actually did
case.body: At 07:15 you won Denzel Boston, Jonah Coleman, Eddy Pineiro and the Vikings D/ST, and gave up Brian Thomas Jr., Kyle Pitts, Tyler Loop and the Ravens D/ST. Winning three claims early pushed you to last in the order, which is why the Brock Purdy claim lost to Los Gigantes de Teca at priority 6.

case.label: Why that closes today
case.body: Standing policy closes any slot that changed hands inside seven days unless a player in it is ruled out. Four slots are inside that window, and the two names most tempting to re-claim — Pitts at 90.1% rostered and Thomas at 77.6% — are the two you dropped this morning. Re-claiming either is a same-day reversal from the back of the queue.

case.label: Falsified if
case.body: Baltimore rule Zay Flowers out on Friday, which arms the Bateman card below; or Minnesota lose pass rushers on Thursday's first full injury report, which would reopen the defence seat you just filled.

doFirst.deadlineLabel: Fallback only — do not fire today
doFirst.title: If Baltimore rule Zay Flowers out, add Rashod Bateman for Jonah Coleman
doFirst.subtitle: Bateman is a free agent here, so this costs a roster move and nothing else. It is unarmed because Flowers is currently expected to play.

case.label: The player
case.body: In Week 2 without Flowers, Bateman played 93% of Baltimore's snaps and no other Ravens receiver cleared 55%. He led the team in targets, catches and receiving yards, caught their only passing touchdown, and finished with 21.8 PPR points. Baltimore host Dallas, who sit 31st in coverage.

case.label: Why it is not armed
case.body: NBC Sports reported on 21 September that Flowers, with a hamstring, has a "good shot" to play against Dallas. Every number above was produced in his absence. With Flowers on the field, Bateman's 93% snap share is a one-week artifact and he is a WR4 on a run-first offence.

case.label: The drop
case.body: Jonah Coleman is the only name on your bench that this clears. He arrived six hours ago on a claim, so dropping him is a same-day reversal — which is precisely why this card is a fallback rather than an instruction. It only becomes right if Denver also clear J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey, which would collapse the lead-back role Coleman was claimed for.

case.label: Falsified if
case.body: Flowers practises in full on Friday or is anything better than out — then this card never fires. It is also falsified if Denver rule Dobbins and Harvey out again, which makes Coleman the keeper and leaves no drop candidate at all.

whatWentWrong.title: The Purdy claim lost, and Kyle Pitts was spent anyway
whatWentWrong.lead: Los Gigantes de Teca took Brock Purdy at priority 6. You went to priority 10 by winning three claims first, and Pitts left the roster on the claim that did land.

case.label: The mechanism
case.body: ESPN processes claims in priority order and drops a team to the back of the queue the moment it wins one. You entered at 2 of 10, won Boston, Pineiro and the Vikings, and by the time Purdy was reached you were behind Los Gigantes. The league file now shows Purdy on their roster at slot 0 and you at waiverRank 10.

case.label: What it cost
case.body: Kyle Pitts, 90.1% rostered nationally, left for Jonah Coleman at 38.0% owned and a 1.7 weekly projection. The quarterback the drop was meant to buy went elsewhere. That is the whole cost of stacking four claims behind one you wanted most.

case.label: What it changes now
case.body: Nothing to reverse — Atlanta named Michael Penix Jr. their Thursday starter on Monday, so Pitts is no longer the third-string-quarterback trap he was when the card was written. But standing policy says not to carry a second tight end in Chem at all, because the flex here is RB/WR only. See the Do-not-chase row.

case.label: What would change it
case.body: If a future claim queue matters, file the single claim you most want first rather than stacking four — priority is consumed by the first win, not by the last.

whatWentWrong.title: Brian Thomas Jr. was the drop, not Kyle Monangai
whatWentWrong.lead: The published card paired Denzel Boston with dropping Monangai. The claim that executed dropped Thomas instead. Monangai is still on your bench.

case.label: What happened
case.body: Activity at 07:15 reads WAIVER_ADD Denzel Boston, WAIVER_DROP Brian Thomas Jr. Thomas is now on waivers at 77.6% owned, clearing Thursday 01:00 Mexico City, and you are last in the queue for him.

case.label: Whether it was wrong
case.body: The thesis that held Thomas for four runs had already broken. His route share sits at 74%, behind both Jakobi Meyers at 88% and Parker Washington at 90%, and Washington — not Thomas — led Jacksonville's receiving in Week 1. Meyers drew one target in Week 2, so the old Meyers-based clause was measuring the wrong man. The drop was defensible; it just was not the drop the card named.

case.label: Why not re-claim him
case.body: Reversing a move made six hours ago from the back of the waiver order is the churn pattern standing policy names explicitly. He would also cost the roster spot Boston now occupies, and Boston has the better two-week profile: seven catches, 154 yards and two touchdowns on 11 targets.

case.label: What would change it
case.body: Thomas clearing waivers unclaimed on Thursday and reverting to free agency, at which point he costs no priority — and only then if his route share crosses 85% against New England.

whatWentWrong.title: ESPN projects Jonah Coleman at 1.7 and reporting has him leading Denver's backfield
whatWentWrong.lead: The number on your own bench row is the one to disbelieve this week. Read the role, not the projection.

case.label: What reporting says
case.body: FantasyPros' Week 3 waiver column has Coleman emerging as Denver's lead back after injuries to J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey: 10 carries for 39 yards and a touchdown plus three catches on three targets, on 25 snaps, nine more than Tyler Badie. CBS listed him a must-add at 15% FAAB and 49% rostered.

case.label: What ESPN says
case.body: 1.7 projected points, which is a backup's number. Both Dobbins and Harvey are listed questionable rather than out on rosters in this league, so the projection is most likely pricing their return rather than Coleman's Week 2 role.

case.label: Which to believe
case.body: Believe the reporting on the role and the projection on the risk. He is a bench stash in a RB/WR flex you already fill with Jalen Coker, so the disagreement costs you nothing this week — but it is the reason he is not a drop candidate for anyone.

case.label: What would change it
case.body: Denver clearing Dobbins or Harvey to full practice by Friday, which would make the 1.7 the honest number and open Coleman's roster spot.

worthALook.name: Tre Tucker
worthALook.lead: Five catches, 119 yards and a touchdown on seven targets at the Chargers in Week 2, and he is a free agent here.

case.label: The case
case.body: CBS listed him a Week 3 waiver target at 50% rostered nationally and 10% FAAB, calling him a reliable No. 3 receiver even with Brock Bowers returning. He is free-agent status in Chem, so he costs no waiver priority at all — only a roster spot.

case.label: Why he is not a card
case.body: Your bench is Tuten, McLaurin, Monangai, Boston and Coleman, and four of those five are either inside the seven-day churn window or carry an intact reason for being there. There is no drop that clears the bar today, and an add without a named drop is not a recommendation.

case.label: The honest risk
case.body: Week 1 was a dud against Miami and the Week 2 line came with a touchdown, which is the noise half of the signal. Bowers coming back is a genuine target competitor, not a formality.

case.label: What would change it
case.body: Monangai losing the Chicago backfield outright on Monday night, or Coleman's Denver role collapsing when Dobbins and Harvey are cleared — either opens the bench seat this needs.

worthALook.name: Xavier Worthy
worthALook.lead: Carried forward from yesterday unchanged, and with an honest gap: no usable role reporting surfaced for him this run.

case.label: The anomaly
case.body: 75.0% rostered nationally and a free agent in a ten-team league, projecting 11.5 this week on a 165.6 season number. That is the ownership-anomaly band, which standing policy rates the strongest single wire signal in a shallow league.

case.label: What I could not find
case.body: Searches for his Week 3 target share and role returned Chiefs-team pieces about Rashee Rice and no usable per-game numbers for Worthy himself. That is a finding, not an omission: the row stays open but no card can be built on it, because recommending a claim on ownership alone is the failure mode this log already records twice.

case.label: The standing decline
case.body: He was declined on 19 September on Kansas City's air-yards profile and that decision has not been revisited with new evidence. Nothing this run contradicts it.

case.label: What would change it
case.body: Two things, unchanged from the original decline: Kansas City's air-yards profile normalising across two weeks, or Rashee Rice missing time. Rice is off Kansas City's injury report, so that second branch stays shut.

doNotChase.name: Kyle Pitts Sr.
doNotChase.lead: You dropped him this morning and the instinct to buy him back is the wrong one, even though Penix is now the quarterback.

case.label: What changed in his favour
case.body: Atlanta named Michael Penix Jr. their Thursday starter on Monday, a full participant in the estimated practice report. Cooper Rush, who started the first two games, completed 56.4% with a league-high four interceptions. The third-string-quarterback risk that justified dropping Pitts is gone.

case.label: The number that kills it
case.body: Chem's flex is RB/WR only — slot id 3. A second tight end cannot enter your lineup in any week of this season. Standing policy says do not carry one here at all, and that is a structural fact, not a projection.

case.label: The queue
case.body: He is on waivers at 90.1% rostered clearing Thursday 01:00 Mexico City, and you are priority 10 of 10. You would very likely lose the claim and burn the drop anyway.

case.label: What would change it
case.body: Isaiah Likely appearing on a Giants injury report. That, and only that, makes a second tight end necessary rather than unusable.

doNotChase.name: Jaxson Dart
doNotChase.lead: 83.0% rostered and sitting on your waiver wire is the strongest ownership anomaly on the board. It is also a trap.

case.label: Why he looks free
case.body: He is the single most widely rostered player available in either league and his ownership is falling 10.95 points in a day, which is what a managed exodus looks like rather than a blunder.

case.label: The number that kills it
case.body: Initial X-rays on Monday showed an MCL sprain. Tuesday's MRI came back worse than anticipated and Ian Rapoport reported him out an extended period, possibly the season. Jameis Winston is the Giants' starter going forward. Dart's weekly projection in this file is 0.0 while his season projection still reads 256.2 — availability is the one thing that number does not price.

case.label: The cost
case.body: A claim from priority 10 that you would probably lose, spending a drop on a quarterback who may not play again in 2026, when you already start the league's QB1.

case.label: What would change it
case.body: The Giants publishing a dated return. Nothing short of that.

doNotChase.name: Dalton Schultz
doNotChase.lead: The biggest single ownership move on the entire Chem wire, and it is aimed at a slot you do not have.

case.label: Why the market moved
case.body: Plus 23.46 rostered in a day. CBS named him the primary tight end replacement after Dallas Goedert's injury, at 60% rostered nationally. The move is real and the reasoning behind it is sound — for the managers who need a tight end.

case.label: The number that kills it
case.body: You start one tight end and it is Isaiah Likely, who drew ten targets in Week 2. Chem's flex is RB/WR. Schultz's ceiling on your roster is a bench seat you would spend a 55%-owned receiver to create.

case.label: The distinction
case.body: Ownership velocity is a lagging confirmation of a role change, and it is the fourth-best wire signal, not the first. It tells you the market noticed Goedert. It does not tell you the player fits here.

case.label: What would change it
case.body: Likely being ruled out, which would make a startable tight end necessary. Otherwise this row stays a decline every week it appears.

doNotChase.name: Tank Bigsby
doNotChase.lead: He is a live fallback card in IPADE this morning. Here he is nothing, and the cross-league confusion is the trap.

case.label: Why he is rising
case.body: Plus 4.39 rostered in a day. Saquon Barkley took a stinger in Week 2 and DraftKings Network ran the add-Bigsby-or-Shipley question on 22 September. SI call him a solid safety net with a crucial role behind Barkley.

case.label: The number that kills it here
case.body: Barkley is on Panda Attack's roster in Chem, not yours. His handcuff is worth exactly nothing to you unless Bigsby becomes a standalone starter, and his 3.4 weekly projection is what that looks like today.

case.label: Why the row exists at all
case.body: Because the IPADE brief published this morning carries a Bigsby card, and seeing the same name in two briefs is how a right move in one league becomes a wasted roster spot in the other. Same player, opposite answers, for a roster reason.

case.label: What would change it
case.body: Barkley being ruled out for multiple weeks, which would make Bigsby a startable Philadelphia back rather than insurance — and even then he competes with Tuten and Monangai for a bench seat here.

cannotSee.label: seasonProj is live, but it does not price availability
cannotSee.body: seasonProj updates, but it does not price availability. A 21 September run proved the field is live by diffing two commits (245 of 250 season projections changed), so treating it as an August artifact would be wrong. What this run observed is narrower and still matters: it does not reflect availability. Josh Jacobs reads 167.6 while on the commissioner's exempt list and Jaxson Dart reads 256.2 with a possibly season-ending knee, while other injured players are correctly zeroed. Use it to narrow what to research, never as an availability signal or a trade price.

cannotSee.label: No trade is proposed in Chem this week
cannotSee.body: Standing policy says weeks 1 to 3 are noise and to react to role news only. Pricing an offer would also mean naming players on another roster that this run did not research, and no recommendation is made without a search. This is a decision, not an omission.
